Following Apple's announcement of changes to App Tracking Transparency in Europe, the company is now rolling out a simplified App Store commission structure for developers in the region. Here are the details.

Apple overhauls business terms for EU app developers

Apple previously announced eight adjustments to App Tracking Transparency features in Europe, made in response to an investigation by German antitrust regulators.

Apple has now announced that a new commission structure will take effect on October 1 in Europe, including reducing the external link commission to 15% and replacing the controversial Core Technology Fee with a 5% Core Technology Commission.

This move comes more than a year after Apple announced major reforms to its EU App Store, which introduced a series of complex rules. You can learn more about it here.

Below is Apple's statement:

Apple has also announced new terms for App Store commission rates, alternative app payment methods, and app distribution through alternative app marketplaces or the web.

The new terms are as follows:

For App Store apps using Apple's in-app purchase system, the commission will be 26%. For the vast majority of developers—including those participating in the App Store Small Business Program, Mini Apps Partner Program, or Video Partner Program, as well as auto-renewing subscriptions after the first year—the commission will be 15%. For App Store apps using alternative payment processing, the commission will be 20%. Developers in the aforementioned programs will qualify for the lower 10% rate. For App Store apps that link out to a website to complete transactions, the commission will be 15%. Developers in the aforementioned programs will pay the lower 10% rate. For apps distributed through alternative app marketplaces or the web, Apple will charge a 5% Core Technology Commission.

Under the new terms, developers can also offer both Apple's in-app purchase and alternative payment options, whether within the app or via an external link to a website, as long as they meet Apple's 'presentment requirements' and maintain their selected payment option for 12 months.

Today's announcement also includes new child safety protections and alternative payment arrangements in the EU, including:

Apps in the 'Kids' category on the App Store will not contain links that direct users to a website to complete transactions, to reduce the risk of scams or fraud targeting children. For users under 18, all App Store apps using alternative payment processing or linking out to a website to complete transactions must include parental supervision features that require younger users to have a parent or guardian involved before making a purchase. For users under 13, apps on the App Store cannot link out to a website to complete transactions, to prevent the risk of scams targeting young children.

Apple added that in EU member states where children over 13 require parental consent to engage in digital activities, 'these protections will be adjusted accordingly.'

Finally, Apple's latest announced changes also expand eligibility for operating alternative app marketplaces or distributing apps via the web.

The expanded eligibility criteria include:

Meeting a moderate financial stability threshold as rated by Dun & Bradstreet. Being a publicly traded company or owned by one. Having received venture capital funding from a recognized investment institution. Having completed a financial audit by a licensed accountant. Being a government agency, educational institution, or non-profit organization.

Apple noted that the web distribution method currently available only in the EU lacks ongoing oversight from marketplace operators, which could allow bad actors to 'operate for a long time before being discovered, harming user interests.'

Therefore, Apple stated it will continue to require all apps distributed through alternative channels to go through its Notarization process.

To learn more about today's announcement, please visit this link.

Update: In response to a statement from Bloomberg, a European Commission spokesperson welcomed Apple's changes, noting that they were the result of 'close dialogue' with the company. The spokesperson added that the Commission will monitor Apple's implementation of the new terms.

What are your thoughts on Apple's new rules in the EU? Feel free to share them in the comments section.
